list.listitem: Leptospirosis is an acute febrile illness that can progress rapidly with severe sequelae. C
Since leptospirosis is an emerging zoonotic disease widespread in animals, a high index of suspicion is needed in patients with a history suggesting exposure. C
Leptospirosis can be treated with antibiotics, such as penicillin, doxycycline, or other regimens. B

background.definition: Leptospirosis is an emerging infectious disease causing an acute febrile illness of variable severity.

list.listitem: Leptospirosis is considered the most widespread zoonosis in the world.

Reported incidence is 100 to 150 cases per year in the United States, with 50% occurring in Puerto Rico. However, leptospirosis is likely underdiagnosed due to its nonspecific presentation. Leptospirosis was reinstated as a nationally reportable disease in 2013.

Worldwide, outbreaks occur more commonly in crowded urban environments with rat infestations and limited sanitation services. In the United States, most outbreaks occur following recreational freshwater or occupational animal exposure, although cases of leptospirosis have been reported after hurricanes.

A 2007 outbreak in Germany among 153 strawberry workers (13 confirmed cases and 11 suspected) was attributed to an unusually warm winter combined with contact between hand lesions and contaminated water or soil and infected voles.
Most reported cases occur in men, which may reflect higher exposure rates or sex differences in severity.
Leptospirosis outbreaks occur following periods of environmental perturbation such as heavy rains, hurricanes and similar weather events that cause flooding.
Leptospirosis is caused by spirochete bacteria of the genus Leptospira. Numerous serovars cause disease in humans. Many genomes have been completely sequenced.
Leptospires are transmitted in the urine of various animals, most commonly rats. People can be infected via ingestion or direct contact between microabrasions and contaminated freshwater or soil.

Leptopsirosis presentation can range from a mild self-limited febrile illness to a fulminant life-threatening illness involving multiple organ systems.Incubation period is approximately 10 days, with a range of 2 to 20 days, after which illness lasts days to weeks.
Although most patients recover completely, case fatality rates in severe leptospirosis are 10% to 50%; the mechanism of pathogenesis is not well understood.

Where leptospirosis risk is high, doxycycline is believed to be useful as prophylaxis, but data are conflicting. BChemoprophylaxis may be indicated for select groups such as soldiers deployed to high-risk areas, people involved in extreme outdoor sports or dairy farmers who have heavily infected herds. C
No human vaccine is available in the United States. C
One randomized trial of 800 farm workers in Sri Lanka (penicillin 500 mg twice daily or placebo) demonstrated 3 cases of leptospirosis, all in the placebo group.

A Cochrane review in 2024, based on low to very low certainty evidence, was unable to determine whether the use of antibiotics to prevent leptospirosis in travelers and high-risk groups affects all-cause mortality and whether it causes adverse events.
Patients typically present with abrupt onset of continuous high fevers and often have malaise, myalgias, headache, GI symptoms, jaundice, and conjunctivitis. C
Specific testing for leptospirosis is indicated when history suggests exposure, other work-up is nondiagnostic, and illness is worsening or severe. C
Serology is the easiest initial screen. Various commercial kits are available. Both ELISA and PCR are useful as initial tests. B
The microscopic agglutination test (MAT) is the reference method, and it is most useful as a confirmatory test. C
Leptospirosis causes abrupt onset fevers (99% of patients).

Other common signs and symptoms are malaise, myalgias (91%), headache (89%), chills (87%), nausea/vomiting (75%), and arthralgias (59%). Less common symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and backache (about 50% of patients), conjunctival suffusion (28%), nuchal rigidity (27%), oliguria or anuria (26%), pneumonia (17%), or rash (8%).
More serious clinical manifestations include jaundice (39%), hepatomegaly (16%), splenomegaly (4%), thrombocytopenia, anemia, and altered mental status.
Icterohemorrhagic leptospirosis, or Weil syndrome, is the most severe form and occurs with renal and hepatic failure or pulmonary hemorrhages.

Initial laboratory tests should include CBC, creatinine, liver enzymes, and urinalysis. Routine blood cultures have low sensitivity for spirochetes and do not rule out leptospirosis if negative. Abnormal BUN or creatinine, hematuria, and proteinuria are seen in about half of patients and about 3 in 4 have elevated bilirubin and ALT. In the largest reported series 39% had elevated WBC and 7% had decreased WBC.
Lumbar puncture is recommended to rule out other infections in patients with meningeal signs.
Specific testing for leptospirosis is indicated if illness is severe or worsening.
ELISA is the most readily available test to detect antibodies.
MAT is the reference method and detects antibodies against specific serovars. A positive test is a single titer of more than 1:400 or a 4-fold rise between acute and convalescent sera.

PCR is highly specific and the most sensitive method in initial serum samples when other tests are negative. A Cochrane review found significant between-study variability in the accuracy of PCR as well as significant variability in disease prevalence between studies. Additionally, the authors found insufficient evidence for the accuracy of nucleic acid and antigen detection tests for leptospirosis.

In a review of 124 Brazilian patients, ELISA and a slide agglutination test had the best initial sensitivity. All tests were sensitive between 9 and 14 days, but sensitivity then dropped after 2 weeks of illness. PCR and MAT are the most specific tests.
Leptospirosis can be difficult to distinguish clinically from other acute febrile illnesses.

Suspect leptospirosis with an abrupt onset of fever, chills, conjunctival suffusion, headache, myalgia, and jaundice, without another clear diagnosis. Clinical suspicion should increase in patients with a history of occupational or recreational exposure to freshwater or animal urine.

The initial screening test is usually serologic, with ELISA most easily available. Several relatively inexpensive commercial kits are available using simple methods such as a dipstick that can be performed locally. MAT may be performed as a confirmatory test. Concurrent initial testing by PCR improves the sensitivity of diagnosis.
The antibiotics of choice based on limited clinical trial and sensitivity data are penicillin and doxycycline. B
Cefotaxime and azithromycin have been shown to be equivalent to doxycycline and/or penicillin in 2 RCTs. B
Quinolones have been suggested as alternatives, but clinical trial data are lacking. C

A Cochrane review in 2024, based on very low certainty evidence, was unable to determine whether the use of antibiotics to treat leptospirosis affects all-cause mortality and what adverse effects it causes, both minor or serious. B
Leptospirosis is generally treated with antibiotics, although evidence is scarce for the effectiveness of any regimen.
Treatment within a few days after onset of illness may be preferable, but this has not been studied well.
Penicillin is the traditional treatment of choice for severe disease. Doxycycline is the traditional alternate, especially for moderate or mild disease.
New trials suggest that cephalosporins, azithromycin, and quinolones hold promise.

In an RCT comparing penicillin, doxycycline, and cefotaxime in 540 patients in Thailand with severe leptospirosis, the mortality rate, duration of fever, progression of organ failure, and treatment tolerance were similar for all 3 study groups. Doses were penicillin G 1.5 million units IV q 6 hours, cefotaxime 1 g IV q 6 hours, or doxycycline 200 g IV slowly over 30 minutes followed by 100 mg IV q 12 hours.
Another RCT of 80 patients in Thailand presenting with acute fever later determined to be leptospirosis found that 3 days of oral azithromycin were as efficacious as 7 days of oral doxycycline.

A Cochrane review in 2024, based on very low certainty evidence, was unable to determine whether the use of antibiotics to treat leptospirosis affects all-cause mortality and what adverse effects it causes, both minor or serious.
Hospitalization is indicated for evidence of severe or ongoing end-organ damage to the brain, kidneys, liver, or lungs.
Leptospirosis causes an acute febrile illness that is often self-limited but may be highly variable over days to weeks. C
Leptospirosis in its most severe form may have mortality rates as high as 50% from renal, hepatic, or pulmonary failure. B
Three clinical features predict severe disease or mortality—lung involvement, cardiac damage clinically or on ECG, and clinical jaundice.
Several inflammatory markers are associated with mortality including long pentraxin PTX3 and the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-8; PTX3 was also associated with disease severity.
Cases of congenital leptospirosis or fetal death have been reported only rarely.
Children younger than 8 should receive an alternative to doxycycline.
